newsitem.title: USA: US senators dismayed North Korea food swap failed.
newsitem.headline: US senators dismayed North Korea food swap failed.

text.p: North Korea's cancellation of a zinc-for-wheat barter complicates its murky food supply situation and may be a sign the famine-threatened nation is in worse shape than thought, U.S. senators said Thurday.

"It's clear they don't have any foreign cash reserves," said Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican. He said North Korea had been "thoroughly uncooperative" with attempts to guage its food needs.
Senator Max Baucus, who visited Pyongyang last week, called the decision "very unfortunate."

Baucus, a Montana Democrat, told reporters that he stressed to officials, including the North Korean foreign minister, that "it would be very appropriate...to arrange commercial transactions" in addition to humanitarian food aid.
But as he left Pyongyang on May 28, "it was becoming apparent the (barter) deal was falling through."
"I asked why. I got no answer," Baucus said.

North Korean officials repeated their preference for self-reliance but also said they needed food aid. Baucus said he urged North Korea to enter into proposed four-nation talks intended to bring peace to the Korean peninsula.

Senator Pat Leahy, Vermont Democrat and an Agriculture Committee member, said he had believed North Korea's secretive government and its shaky condition meant any food sales deal would be "difficult at best."
"I suspect North Korea is in even worse condition than we think," Leahy said.

Leahy said trade speculation -- that North Korea was unable to produce the 4,000 tonnes of zinc to barter for 20,000 tonnes of wheat -- sounded plausible "or somebody decided they didn't like the deal."
Lugar said loss of the sale "complicataes the nutritional situation in North Korea." The barter would have equaled 10 percent of food aid now being sought by the United Nations for North Korea.
The international community probably will have to make a new assessment of what needs to be done in aid, Lugar said. So far, it has been difficult to size up the extent of hunger.
"My judgement is our government played it just about right," Lugar said.
If a large portion of the population faces hunger, "something much larger than what we have been talking about will be needed," he said.
Leahy said it was not in the moral or strategic interest of the United States to allow starvation.
